Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals (Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $S$ is bounded
   above (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), then $(x_k)$ converges (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) supplies the
first and Every nonempty set bounded below has an infimum the second, and each is unique
(Suprema and infima are unique).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

derivations.claim: 1.1 If $S=G$, all costs and values are zero, and the theorem follows. Otherwise let $S\setminus G\ne\emptyset$. For any history-dependent policy, finite state/action histories form finite discrete spaces at each time, so the conditional action and transition rules are probability kernels. By [A1] and [F2], the corresponding trajectory law exists with the specified finite-prefix probabilities; this justifies the expectations in the Statement. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Define the Bellman map $T$ by $(Tu)(g)=0$ on goals and $(Tu)(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)u(s')]$ off goals. Set $f_0(s)=0$ and $f_{n+1}=Tf_n$. The minimum is attained by [F3]. These are finite-horizon optimal costs: for $n=0$ the continuation cost is zero; if the claim holds at horizon $n$, conditioning on the first action and next state gives the displayed recursion at horizon $n+1$. Any randomized first action gives a convex combination of action costs, which is at least their minimum; a minimizing pure action attains that minimum, so the finite-horizon optimum is the displayed value. [given, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 The recursion is monotone in its value argument because all transition weights are nonnegative, and $f_1\ge f_0=0$; induction gives $0\le f_n\le f_{n+1}$. For any stationary policy $\pi$, let $U=S\setminus G$ and define the substochastic matrix $Q^\pi$ on $U$ by $Q^\pi(s,t)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(t\mid s,a)$. The properness recursion gives $q_0^\pi|_U=\mathbf 1$ and $q_{n+1}^\pi|_U=Q^\pi q_n^\pi|_U$, so $q_n^\pi|_U=(Q^\pi)^n\mathbf 1$; since $Q^\pi\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$, these survival probabilities are nonincreasing. For the proper stationary policy $\bar\pi$ in the Given assumptions, choose $N_s\ge1$ with $q_{N_s}^{\bar\pi}(s)<1$ for each state. Since $S$ is finite, $N=\max_sN_s$ and $\rho=\max_s q_N^{\bar\pi}(s)$ satisfy $\rho<1$. Also $q_N^{\bar\pi}(s)=\sum_{t\in U}(Q^{\bar\pi})^N(s,t)$ for $s\in U$, and $q_{(k+1)N}^{\bar\pi}=(Q^{\bar\pi})^Nq_{kN}^{\bar\pi}$. Thus induction gives $q_{kN}^{\bar\pi}(s)\le\rho^k$ for every state and $k\ge0$. The finite maximum $c_{\max}=\max\{c(s,a):s\in U,\ a\in A(s)\}$ exists by [F3]. During block $k$, each stage cost has expectation at most $c_{\max}q_{kN}^{\bar\pi}(s)\le c_{\max}\rho^k$, because survival decreases in time. Hence $J^{\bar\pi}(s)\le Nc_{\max}\sum_{k\ge0}\rho^k=Nc_{\max}/(1-\rho)$. Since $f_n$ is the $n$-step optimum, $f_n(s)\le J^{\bar\pi}(s)$; thus each increasing sequence $f_n(s)$ is bounded above, and [F4] gives a finite limit $f(s)$. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Passing to the limit in the finite sums and finite minima in step 1.2 is valid coordinatewise; the minimum of finitely many convergent real sequences converges to the minimum of their limits. Hence $f(g)=0$ on $G$ and $f(s)=\min_a[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)f(s')]$ off $G$. Therefore $f$ is a finite nonnegative Bellman fixed point. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Enumerate the finite state set as $s_1,\ldots,s_m$. For each nonglobal state, [F3] gives a nonempty finite set of actions minimizing the fixed-point expression in step 3.1. Inductively along this finite list, select one minimizer at each state; at each successor stage one nonempty finite set is added to the already chosen finite tuple, so this finite construction uses no arbitrary-index choice. The selected actions define a deterministic stationary policy $\pi^*$. For $n=0$ the identity is $f(s)=f(s)$. If it holds at $n$, condition on the next state and apply the Bellman equality at the current state to obtain it at $n+1$; hence induction gives $f(s)=\mathbb E_s^{\pi^*}[\sum_{t<n}c(S_t,A_t)1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}+f(S_n)]$ for every $n$. By step 2.1 and [F4], the survival probabilities under $\pi^*$ have a limit; if that limit were $q_\infty>0$, the partial cost expectation would be at least $n c_{\min}q_\infty$, contradicting the finite left side and nonnegative terminal term. Thus $\pi^*$ is proper. Since $f$ is bounded on finite $S$ and $f=0$ on $G$, properness gives $\mathbb E_s^{\pi^*}f(S_n)\le\max_xf(x)q_n^{\pi^*}(s)\to0$; letting $n\to\infty$ in the identity yields $J^{\pi^*}(s)=f(s)$. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix an initial state $s$ and any policy $\sigma$. The fixed-point equation gives $f(x)\le c(x,a)+\sum_{x'}P(x'\mid x,a)f(x')$ for each nonglobal $x$ and every action $a$, with equality at goals. Averaging over each history-dependent action distribution gives the one-step inequality; conditioning successively on the finite-prefix laws and inducting on $n$ gives $f(s)\le\mathbb E_s^\sigma[\sum_{t<n}c(S_t,A_t)1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}+f(S_n)]$. Under $\sigma$, the events $\{S_n\notin G\}$ decrease because goals are absorbing. If their probabilities tend to zero, boundedness of the terminal term makes $f(s)\le J^\sigma(s)$. If they do not tend to zero, their limit is positive, and the positive cost lower bound makes $J^\sigma(s)=+\infty$; again $f(s)\le J^\sigma(s)$. Thus $f$ is a lower bound for every policy cost, while step 4.1 exhibits a policy attaining it. Consequently $f=f^*$. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $g$ be any finite nonnegative solution of the same Bellman equations. Since $f_0=0\le g$, the monotonicity of $T$ from step 2.1 gives $f_n=T^n0\le T^ng=g$ for every $n$, hence $f^*\le g$. The Bellman minimum for $g$ is no larger than any action value, so $g(x)\le c(x,a)+\sum_{x'}P(x'\mid x,a)g(x')$ for every nonglobal $x$ and action $a$. Average this inequality along the proper policy $\pi^*$ from step 4.1 and iterate over $n$ steps to obtain $g(s)\le\mathbb E_s^{\pi^*}[\sum_{t<n}c(S_t,A_t)1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}+g(S_n)]$. The terminal term tends to zero because $g$ is bounded and $\pi^*$ is proper, so $g(s)\le J^{\pi^*}(s)=f^*(s)$. Therefore $g=f^*$, proving uniqueness. [given, F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Input: a finite stochastic shortest-path model, a finite value table $V_0:S\to\mathbb R$ with $V_0(g)=0$ on goals, a nonempty finite start set $S_0\subseteq S\setminus G$, a positive integer trial cap $L$, and an infinite supplied start sequence in which each member of $S_0$ occurs infinitely often. For each trial, set the current state to the next supplied start. For at most $L$ decision steps, or until a goal is reached, do the following: at the current nonglobal state $s$, compute

$$q_V(s,a)=r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\qquad(a\in A(s)),$$

choose uniformly from the nonempty set of actions attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using a fresh tie draw, execute the chosen action in the given MDP and observe the next state, then replace $V(s)$ by $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using the value table from before that backup. Keep every other value unchanged. At a goal keep value $0$. After a trial ends, reset the state to the next supplied start without resetting the value table. The procedure returns the successive value tables and selected actions; it asserts no convergence guarantee by itself.

From $y$ and $z$ the goal is reached deterministically. Thus this is a finite positive-cost SSP with a proper stationary policy. At $x$ there is no action choice; its survival probability after $n$ steps is $2^{-n}$, so its expected total cost is $\sum_{n=0}^\infty2^{-n}=2$ by the finite geometric identity and its limit. The deterministic costs at $y,z$ and the sole initial choice at $s$ therefore give $f^*(z)=1$, $f^*(y)=1+f^*(z)=2$, and $f^*(s)=\min\{1+f^*(x),1+f^*(y)\}=3$. The initial table is finite, zero at the goal, and no larger than these optimal costs.

Induct on the number $k$ of completed trials. At the first trial, $f_0(x)=0<2=f_0(y)$. If $y$ has not been visited in the first $k$ trials and $x$ has been backed up $k$ times, then $f_k(y)=2$ and the recurrence $f_{j+1}(x)=1+\frac12f_j(x)$, obtained from the sole action at $x$ and $f_j(g)=0$, gives $f_k(x)=2(1-2^{-k})<2$. Thus action $a$ has cost $1+f_k(x)<3$, whereas action $b$ has cost $1+f_k(y)=3$. Since $V=-f$ and $r=-c$, the RTDP reward-greedy rule is cost-minimizing; it therefore uniquely chooses $a$ at $s$. The next trial moves to $x$ and does not visit $y$. The cap $L=2$ then provides exactly one backup at $x$, completing the induction. Tie-breaking is never invoked at $s$.

Each trial first executes $a$ and moves to $x$. With cap $L=2$, RTDP then executes the sole action at $x$ and backs up $x$ once before the trial ends, whether that transition returns to $x$ or reaches $g$. Thus the recurrence in step 2.1 holds on every trial, and neither $y$ nor $z$ is ever visited or backed up. In particular, the estimate of $z$ remains $0$ forever although $f^*(z)=1$.

For the goal-terminated variant, after any finite total number $m$ of backups at $x$, its cost is $2(1-2^{-m})<2$. Thus every later departure from $s$ still uniquely selects $a$. Each trial then consists of visits to $x$ until its transition to $g$; the probability of at least $n$ self-transitions is $2^{-n}$, which tends to zero, so the trial is finite almost surely. The union over the countably many trials of their zero-probability nontermination events has probability zero by countable subadditivity. On the complementary event every finite trial boundary has only finitely many backups at $x$, so the strict inequality persists. Neither $y$ nor $z$ is ever visited, and $f(z)=0$ forever.

The stationary policy that chooses $b$ at $s$ and then follows the sole actions at $y$ and $z$ has total cost $1+2=3=f^*(s)$, so it is optimal from the designated start $s$ and reaches $z$ with probability one. Hence $z$ is optimal-relevant by the stated definition, but its estimate fails to converge on every capped run by step 3.1 and almost surely on goal-terminated runs by step 3.2. This refutes the claimed almost-sure convergence on all optimal-relevant states, and therefore also refutes the conjunction with the source's claimed eventual optimality on every such state.

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. Let $M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},r,P)$ and $\widehat M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},\widehat r,\widehat P)$ be finite models on a common nonempty finite state set and common nonempty finite action sets, with $r,\widehat r\in[0,1]$ and probability transition rows. Let $d_t$ and $\widehat d_t$ be the state occupancies under $M$ and $\widehat M$, respectively, starting from $d_0=\widehat d_0=\mu$. Define

$$C_H^\pi=\{(s,a): d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\text{ or }\widehat d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\text{ for some }0\le t<H\}.$$

Its finite reward alphabet is contained in $[0,1]$, so $r(s,a)\in[0,1]$, and $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution on $S$ for every admissible pair. Let $\widehat M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},\widehat r,\widehat P)$ be a finite learned model on the same domain, with $\widehat r(s,a)\in[0,1]$ and a probability distribution $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every admissible pair. Set $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. Let $B\subseteq D$ be the pairs observed at least once in a data set, fix a horizon $H\ge1$ and initial state law $\mu$, and let $\Pi$ be any finite nonempty class of deterministic time-dependent Markov policies for that horizon. For a policy $\pi\in\Pi$, compute its expected return under the true model and learned model using $d_0=\mu$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a),\qquad J_H(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a),$$

and analogously $\widehat J_H(\pi)$ using $\widehat P,\widehat r$. The learned-model occupancy of a pair $(s,a)$ at time $t$ is $\widehat d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)$. A model-optimal policy is any $\widehat\pi\in\Pi$ attaining $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat J_H(\pi)$. Such a policy **exploits the model off support relative to $B$** if it has positive learned-model occupancy on at least one pair in $D\setminus B$, overestimates its own true return $\widehat J_H(\widehat\pi)>J_H(\widehat\pi)$, and is truly suboptimal within $\Pi$: $J_H(\widehat\pi)<\max_{\pi\in\Pi}J_H(\pi)$. This definition describes a failure mode; it is not a performance claim about every model optimizer.

$$Q_h(s,a)=\hat r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}\hat P(s'\mid s,a)V_{h-1}(s'),\qquad V_h(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q_h(s,a).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let a finite positive-cost stochastic shortest-path problem have at least one proper stationary policy. For any policy $\sigma$ whose action distribution may depend on the entire finite history, use its trajectory law from the initial state $s$ and define

$$J^\sigma(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E_s^\sigma\!\left[c(S_t,A_t)\,1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}\right],$$

$$f^*(g)=0\quad(g\in G),\qquad f^*(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}\left[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)f^*(s')\right]\quad(s\notin G).$$

The minimum is attained by a deterministic stationary policy that is proper and has total cost $f^*$ from every initial state.

derivations.claim: 1.1 Bellman monotonicity and [F2] imply $f_n\le f^*$ after every backup: an updated value is no greater than the same backup of $f^*$, and other values do not change. Put $e_n=f^*-f_n\ge0$ and $\delta(s,a)=c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)f^*(t)-f^*(s)\ge0$. An update at $s$ gives $e_{n+1}(s)=\max_a\{\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)e_n(t)-\delta(s,a)\}$. Consequently $\max_s e_n(s)$ is nonincreasing and all errors are bounded by their finite initial maximum. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 We first justify the probability-one recurrence fact used below. At each of the successive opportunities when a fixed pair $(s,a)$ is currently greedy at a backed state $s$, the conditional probability of selecting $a$ is at least $1/|A(s)|$. For any finite number $m$ of such opportunities after a fixed index, iterated conditioning [F4] bounds the probability of avoiding $a$ through all of them by $(1-1/|A(s)|)^m$; for random opportunity times, first stop at a finite horizon and then increase the horizon, so the same inequality holds on the event those opportunities exist. Letting $m$ increase proves that infinitely many opportunities imply infinitely many selections almost surely. At successive selections of a fixed $(s,a)$, the same argument with probability $P(t\mid s,a)>0$ shows that successor $t$ occurs infinitely often almost surely. Countably many tail indices and finitely many states/actions/successors allow one common probability-one event for all these implications. [given, A1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Work on that event. Since there are finitely many states, after some finite index only states in $I$ are backed. An action greedy at infinitely many backups of a state in $I$ is selected infinitely often by step 1.2. Every nonglobal positive-probability successor is then an outcome infinitely often, hence belongs to $I$ by outcome-backup fairness. There are only finitely many remaining state-action pairs, so after another finite index every minimizing action at every backed state has transition support in $I\cup G$. In particular, after this index the errors of any successors used by a minimizing action are errors inside $I$, or zero goal errors. [given, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Let $E_n=\max_{s\in I}e_n(s)$ after the index in step 2.1. The set $I$ is nonempty because infinitely many backups occur on a finite state set. The maximum is attained on a finite set. Choose any minimizing action at the current backed state; the error identity in step 1.1, evaluated at that action, and step 2.1 give its post-backup error at most $E_n$. Unupdated errors stay fixed. Hence $E_n$ is nonincreasing, nonnegative, and has a finite limit $E$ by [F5]. [given, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Suppose $E>0$ and put $J=\{s\in I:\limsup_n e_n(s)=E\}$. Finiteness and attainment of the maxima imply $J$ is nonempty. Each $s\in J$ is backed infinitely often and its value is constant between backups, so some sequence of its post-backup errors tends to $E$. On a subsequence one fixed minimizing action $a_s$ realizes these backups, since the action set is finite. In the error identity from step 1.1 its successor errors are all at most $E_n\to E$, by step 2.1; attaining limiting error $E$ forces $\delta(s,a_s)=0$, excludes positive-probability goal successors, and forces every positive-probability successor to have limsup error $E$. Thus every successor lies in $J$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Select one such $a_s$ at each member of finite $J$ by finite enumeration. These actions are globally Bellman-optimal and keep every finite transition law in $J$. Iterating their Bellman equalities for $m$ steps gives $f^*(s)=\mathbb E_s[\sum_{k<m}c(S_k,a_{S_k})+f^*(S_m)]\ge m c_{\min}$ by [F1] and nonnegativity of $f^*$. This contradicts finiteness of $f^*(s)$ for large $m$. Therefore $E=0$, giving uniform convergence on $I$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra, contradiction]

6.1 Any action greedy at infinitely many backups has support in $I\cup G$ by step 2.1. Along those backups all successor estimates tend to their optimal values by step 5.1, and the updated state estimate does also. Passing to the limit in its finite Bellman backup proves that its slack $\delta$ is zero. There are finitely many state-action pairs, so after some finite index no action of positive slack is currently minimizing at a backed state. Every designated start is nonglobal by [F3] and belongs to $I$. A stationary policy choosing any eventual minimizing action on $I$ has zero Bellman slack and support in $I\cup G$. For any $s\in I$ and $m\ge1$, iterating its Bellman equalities gives $f^*(s)=\mathbb E_s[\sum_{k<m}c(S_k,A_k)1_{\{S_k\notin G\}}+f^*(S_m)]$. If $q_k=\mathbb P_s(S_k\notin G)$, absorbing goals make $q_k$ nonincreasing, and the identity implies $m c_{\min}q_m\le c_{\min}\sum_{k<m}q_k\le f^*(s)$. Hence $q_m\le f^*(s)/(m c_{\min})\to0$. Since $f^*$ is bounded and zero on $G$, $\mathbb E_s f^*(S_m)\le\max_x f^*(x)q_m\to0$; taking $m\to\infty$ in the identity shows that the policy is proper on $I$ and has total cost $f^*(s)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Suppose additionally $f_0\le Tf_0$. Whenever $f_n\le Tf_n$, each updated coordinate satisfies $f_{n+1}(s)=Tf_n(s)\ge f_n(s)$, while unupdated coordinates are unchanged, so $f_{n+1}\ge f_n$. Monotonicity of $T$ then gives $f_{n+1}\le Tf_{n+1}$: at the updated coordinate $f_{n+1}(s)=Tf_n(s)\le Tf_{n+1}(s)$, and at every unupdated coordinate $f_{n+1}(t)=f_n(t)\le Tf_n(t)\le Tf_{n+1}(t)$. Induction shows that the tables increase coordinatewise and remain subsolutions. They are bounded above by $f^*$ by step 1.1, so on finite $S$ they converge to a finite $\bar f\le f^*$; continuity of finite minima and sums gives $\bar f\le T\bar f$. Every designated start is nonglobal by [F3], is backed infinitely often by hypothesis, and hence belongs to $I$; step 5.1 gives $\bar f=f^*$ there. [given, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 In goal-terminated trials, every nonglobal executed successor is the next backed state before any reset, so outcome-backup fairness holds pathwise. Capped trials are covered precisely when they satisfy the stated fairness condition; no assumption about unvisited optimal branches follows from fresh ties. This proves the trial-schedule assertions. [given, F3, step 6.1]

7.2 If $\bar f(s)=f^*(s)$ and $a$ is globally Bellman-optimal at $s\notin G$, then $f^*(s)=\bar f(s)\le T\bar f(s)\le c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)\bar f(t)=f^*(s)-\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)(f^*(t)-\bar f(t))\le f^*(s)$. Equality throughout forces every positive-probability successor to satisfy $\bar f=f^*$, since $f^*-\bar f\ge0$. [F1, F2, step 6.2, algebra]

8.1 Fix an optimal policy $\sigma$ from a designated start $s_0$. Let $\delta(s,a)=c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)f^*(t)-f^*(s)$, which is nonnegative and zero at goals. For every $n$, [F4] and the conditional transition law give $\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\sum_{k<n}c(S_k,A_k)1_{\{S_k\notin G\}}+f^*(S_n)]=f^*(s_0)+\sum_{k<n}\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\delta(S_k,A_k)]$. Because $J^\sigma(s_0)=f^*(s_0)<\infty$ and costs off goals are at least $c_{\min}$, $\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb P_{s_0}^\sigma(S_k\notin G)\le J^\sigma(s_0)/c_{\min}<\infty$, so these probabilities tend to zero. Boundedness of $f^*$ and $f^*|_G=0$ make the terminal expectation tend to zero; letting $n\to\infty$ in the identity gives $\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\delta(S_k,A_k)]=J^\sigma(s_0)-f^*(s_0)=0$. Thus $\delta(S_k,A_k)=0$ almost surely at every $k$, so every action on a positive-probability prefix of $\sigma$ is globally Bellman-optimal. Starting with $\bar f=f^*$ at $s_0$ and applying step 7.2 along each such prefix proves $\bar f=f^*$ at every state reachable with positive probability under $\sigma$. Since $\sigma$ was arbitrary and $S$ is finite, convergence is uniform on the union of all such reachable states. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 6.2, step 7.2, algebra] ∎
